content.overview: Even a competent analytical method cannot repair a broken sample identity or unknown handling history. Each transfer should preserve who held the sample, its condition and any exceptions.

vocabulary.definition: Documented sequence of sample possession and transfer.
Control capable of revealing unauthorized package access or alteration.
Recorded physical and environmental state relevant to analytical interpretation.

sections.title: Identity follows the sample
sections.body: Unique sample ID, source lot and requested analyses should remain consistent across labels, submission records and laboratory reports.

sections.title: Transfers are attributable and contemporaneous
sections.body: Sender, receiver, date, time, condition and exceptions should be recorded at the transfer rather than reconstructed later.

sections.title: Handling can change the measurand
sections.body: Temperature, moisture exchange, container, hold time and homogenization may affect results and should follow the applicable method or laboratory instruction.

workedExamples: A sample arrives with an intact seal but a mismatched ID; seal integrity does not resolve identity and the discrepancy must be controlled.
commonMistakes: Relabeling without retaining the original linkage.
Ignoring a temperature or package deviation during transport.
content.practicalApplication: Build a chain-of-custody form with source, seal, condition, transfers, receipt acceptance and deviation fields.
content.summary: Sample integrity depends on continuous identity and handling evidence from lot to result.
